nameStory: The Pine Tree Cricket gets its name from its strong association with pine trees, where it spends most of its life singing and feeding. Unlike many crickets that prefer grasses or shrubs, this species has evolved to thrive specifically in the needle-covered branches and bark crevices of pine forests. The scientific name 'pini' directly refers to pines, making this one of the most straightforwardly named crickets in New England.
description: The Pine Tree Cricket is a delicate, pale green to whitish cricket that lives high up in pine trees rather than on the ground like house crickets. These slender insects are about half an inch long with long, thread-like antennae that can be twice their body length. Males have broad, translucent wings that they use like tiny violins to produce their signature chirping songs on warm summer evenings. Their lightweight build and climbing legs make them perfectly adapted for life among pine needles and branches.

idTips.label: Pine tree habitat
idTips.description: Always found in or very near pine trees, often singing from pine branches 10-30 feet above ground where they're nearly impossible to spot

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Pale green to nearly white body that blends perfectly with pine needle undersides, much lighter than most other crickets

idTips.label: Thread-like antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that constantly wave and twitch, often appearing longer than the entire body

idTips.label: Male wing sounds
idTips.description: Males produce a continuous, high-pitched trill that sounds like a tiny bell ringing, much faster and higher than ground crickets

idTips.label: Climbing behavior
idTips.description: Moves with deliberate, careful steps along branches and bark, rarely jumping like ground crickets

idTips.label: Nocturnal activity
idTips.description: Most active and vocal after sunset, when their trilling chorus fills pine forests on warm nights

habitat: Pine Tree Crickets are found in mixed and pure pine forests throughout New England, from coastal pitch pine barrens to mountain white pine stands. They prefer mature trees with thick bark and dense needle cover, often in areas where pine trees form the canopy or significant portions of the forest. You'll find them from sea level to mid-elevation forests, always associated closely with various pine species including white pine, red pine, and pitch pine.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; overwintering eggs begin hatching in late spring as temperatures warm and pine trees start their new growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are singing nightly from pine branches. Males produce their loudest trilling songs during warm July and August evenings.
seasonality.fall: Singing continues into early fall during warm nights, with mating and egg-laying occurring before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard freeze; eggs overwinter in pine bark crevices and will hatch the following spring.

funFact: Pine Tree Crickets are living thermometers - you can calculate the temperature by counting their chirps! Count the number of chirps in 15 seconds, add 40, and you'll get the temperature in Fahrenheit within a few degrees, making them remarkably accurate natural weather instruments.
confusionNotes: Pine Tree Crickets are most easily confused with other tree crickets, but their exclusive pine tree habitat is the key distinguisher - if you hear trilling from deciduous trees or shrubs, it's definitely a different species. Remember: 'Pines equal Pine Tree Crickets' - this species is extremely faithful to its pine tree homes.
contextualKnowledge: Many people assume all crickets live on the ground and are surprised to learn that tree crickets exist at all. Pine Tree Crickets represent a whole different lifestyle from the familiar house crickets or field crickets, having evolved specifically for life in the canopy where they rarely, if ever, touch the ground.
compareHints: Among New England's tree crickets, Pine Tree Cricket is unique in its exclusive preference for pine trees - Snowy Tree Crickets prefer deciduous trees and shrubs, while Broad-winged Tree Crickets favor fruit trees and berry bushes. The Pine Tree Cricket's habitat loyalty makes it the easiest tree cricket to identify, since location tells you almost everything you need to know.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tree crickets, this species stands out for its narrow wing shape compared to the broad-winged tree cricket's obviously wider wings.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Black-horned is the easiest to identify thanks to its dark antennae.

Among New England's tree crickets, the broad-winged species is distinguished by its wider male wings compared to the narrow-winged tree cricket, and its preference for deciduous trees rather than the pine-loving pine tree cricket.
Among New England's tree crickets, the snowy tree cricket has the palest, most translucent appearance.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Four-spotted is the only one with exactly four dark spots on its body.
